title: Divine Mercy
summary: These passages show mercy in the wake of failure, suffering, and need. After Israel’s breach with the golden calf, Exodus 34:6–7 presents God as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and steadfast in love, while also speaking of accountability. Psalm 103 compares God’s compassion to a parent’s tenderness and remembers human frailty. Micah 7 ends with confidence that God pardons wrongdoing and remains faithful. Ephesians 2 describes people who were dead in trespasses being made alive with Christ by mercy and grace; Titus 2 says grace trains people for a changed life. Together, the texts show mercy as more than leniency: it forgives and restores, while also calling people toward transformed conduct.
historical_context: The passages come from different settings. Exodus 34 follows Israel’s covenant breach and Moses’ intercession, when God’s character is proclaimed as the covenant is renewed. Psalm 103 is a song of praise that describes God’s compassion in relation to human frailty. Micah 7 closes with a poetic expression of hope in God’s forgiveness and faithfulness. Ephesians 2 explains salvation through mercy and grace in a letter’s argument; Titus 2 presents grace as a teacher of conduct. These texts connect mercy with both forgiveness and changed life, but they do so in different literary contexts.
canonical_context: Exodus 34 gives a foundational statement of divine compassion after Israel’s breach. Psalm 103 develops that confession by describing God’s compassion toward frail people, and Micah 7 closes with hope that God will forgive and remain faithful. Ephesians 2 and Titus 2 speak of mercy and grace in relation to life and conduct in early Christian communities. The later passages draw on the same broad conviction that God is merciful, but each applies it to its own question rather than simply repeating Exodus.
literary_context: The theme appears in a divine self-proclamation in Exodus 34, a praise song in Psalm 103, a prophetic poem of confidence in Micah 7, and instruction in Ephesians and Titus. Exodus places compassion beside patience, steadfast love, forgiveness, and accountability. Psalm 103 uses a parent-child comparison to explain compassion; Micah ends with a question about a God who pardons; Ephesians 2 contrasts death in trespasses with life in Christ; Titus 2 personifies grace as training its recipients. The forms make mercy visible through confession, praise, hope, and instruction.
covenantal_significance: The passages link divine mercy with restoration and responsibility. Exodus 34 names God’s compassion and forgiveness after Israel’s breach, while also retaining accountability. Psalm 103 emphasizes compassion toward human frailty, and Micah 7 expresses hope in forgiveness and covenant faithfulness. Ephesians 2 describes mercy as the source of new life in Christ; Titus 2 connects grace with a changed way of living. Together these texts present mercy as neither denial of wrongdoing nor permission to remain unchanged: it makes restoration possible and shapes a response.
canonical_role: Divine Mercy serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Divine Mercy in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
